title: Mental health problems: where to find help in Germany
intro: In Germany there are many places to turn to for help with mental health problems, from your family doctor to psychotherapists, outpatient clinics, counselling centres and telephone helplines. The system can seem complicated, and waiting times can be long, but there are routes to quicker help. This article describes the main points of contact in general terms; rules and offers change, so check current details.

sections.heading: First steps
paragraphs: A good first step is a visit to your family doctor, who can assess symptoms, check for physical causes, provide initial treatment and refer you to a specialist. You can also contact a psychotherapist directly. Many therapists offer a first consultation to clarify what kind of help is needed.

sections.heading: Psychotherapy and psychiatry
paragraphs: Statutory health insurance covers psychotherapy by licensed psychotherapists and doctors for recognised conditions such as depression, anxiety disorders and trauma-related problems. Psychiatrists are doctors who can also prescribe medicine. A national appointment service, reached by the number 116117, can help find an appointment for an initial consultation, and many insurers can help look for places too.

sections.heading: Clinics and day services
paragraphs: If symptoms are severe, outpatient psychiatric clinics, day clinics or inpatient treatment at a psychiatric or psychosomatic hospital are available. Rehabilitation programmes may follow. Your doctor can issue a referral, and in emergencies you can go directly to a hospital.

sections.heading: Counselling and self-help
paragraphs: Counselling centres offer advice on addiction, family and relationship problems, stress, debt and other life issues, often at no cost. Self-help groups bring people with similar experiences together. Online programmes and approved digital health applications can offer support while you wait for therapy.

sections.heading: Crisis and emergencies
paragraphs: If you or someone else is in acute danger, call the emergency number 112 or go to the nearest emergency department. Telephone counselling services are available around the clock, free of charge and anonymous, for people in distress. Do not wait if you have thoughts of harming yourself.
Practical issues such as language barriers, insurance status and being a refugee can make access harder. Ask counselling centres about interpreters and about the services you are entitled to.

examples.title: Looking for a therapist
examples.text: Imagine you feel low and anxious for months. You could visit your family doctor, ask about a referral, call the appointment service, and also contact several therapists for a first consultation to shorten waiting time.

examples.title: Helping a friend
examples.text: Suppose a friend tells you they feel hopeless. You might listen without judgment, encourage them to speak to a doctor or counselling service and offer to go with them.
